title: Chirurgie des surfaces conformes : notes manuscrites (s.d., 1983-1984), lettres (1984).

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pages 95–97): Grothendieck classifies real elliptic curves inside his notes on 'surgery of conformal surfaces'. On the previous page a real elliptic curve is encoded as a triple (Π, σ, c). Here Π ≅ Z^2 is the lattice, c is an oriented conformal structure on Π⊗R, and σ is an orientation-reversing involution of Π preserving c. With e_± bases of Π^±, the normal form is Q(x e_+ + y e_-) = x^2 + a y^2, which gives two families E_a and E'_a (a > 0).

This page turns the question around. Start from a complex elliptic curve X = V/Π, with V a complex line. A real structure is an antiholomorphic involution fixing the origin. Such involutions correspond to real forms of V (complex conjugations of V) whose reflection preserves Π. Grothendieck asks two questions: can there be several, and if so are they isomorphic, i.e. conjugate under Aut(X)?

His answer runs as follows. Let G be the group of automorphisms of Π preserving the unoriented conformal class, i.e. similitude-orthogonal maps for Q, of either determinant. Let G^+ = ker(det) = Aut(X, 0), which is cyclic of order 2, 4 or 6. Then:
- X admits a real structure iff det: G → {±1} is surjective, giving 1 → G^+ → G → ±1 → 1.
- An element of G with det −1 is an orthogonal map of the plane with determinant −1, hence a reflection, hence an involution. So it is itself a real structure.
- The real structures are therefore exactly G \ G^+.
- The curves admitting real structures are those whose modular invariant j is real (fixed by complex conjugation).
- In that case G^+ is cyclic of order n = 2, 4 or 6 and G is dihedral of order 2n.

The page ends by proposing to study examples via dihedral groups. On the next page he concludes the following. The set of real structures is a G^+-torsor. Conjugation by G^+ has exactly two orbits (for n = 4, 6: reflections through vertices versus through edges of the square or hexagon). Hence every complex elliptic curve with real j carries exactly two non-isomorphic real structures. He then conjectures that one orbit is of type E_a and the other of type E'_a with the same a.

Modern form: real forms of (X, 0) are classified by H^1(Gal(C/R), Aut X). For n even this has two elements; equivalently, reflections in D_n (n even) form two conjugacy classes. This is classical (Klein, Alling–Greenleaf, Gross–Harris, Silhol).
errors: Imprecision: the problem is posed with 'réseaux' but G must be defined as lattice automorphisms preserving the conformal class up to orientation. Grothendieck has this implicitly from the previous page.
The splitting question raised on the next page is automatic. Every det −1 element is a reflection, hence of order 2, so the sequence always splits once det is surjective.

The conjecture on the next page (the two orbits are E_a and E'_a with the same a) is false in general; it is not on this page but is set up by it. For generic real j (n = 2, G = Klein four group), the two real structures are σ and −σ. These have the same Π^+ ⊕ Π^- splitting type, so both are rectangular (E_a and E_{1/a}) or both rhombic (E'_a and E'_{1/a}). This matches the fact that a quadratic twist by −1 does not change the sign of the discriminant, so both forms have the same number of real components. For the hexagonal lattice (j = 0), y^2 = x^3 + 1 and y^2 = x^3 − 1 both have one real component, so both are rhombic. The 'one E, one E'' pattern holds only for the square lattice (j = 1728: y^2 = x^3 − x vs y^2 = x^3 + x).

ideas.what: Real structures on a complex torus V/Π correspond to reflections (real forms of V) preserving the lattice; existence iff det: G → ±1 is surjective, iff j is real
ideas.modern_name: Real forms of elliptic curves / Galois cohomology H^1(Z/2, Aut X); real j-invariant criterion
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical: F. Klein; Alling–Greenleaf (Klein surfaces, 1971); Gross–Harris (1981); Silhol (1989)
ideas.where_published: Not in his standard published corpus as far as known; the Esquisse d'un programme (1984) mentions real/conformal surfaces and the action of complex conjugation in passing only.

ideas.what: Group G of conformal automorphisms of the lattice of either orientation is dihedral D_n with rotation subgroup Aut(X) = C_n (n = 2, 4, 6); real structures form a G^+-torsor with two conjugacy orbits
ideas.modern_name: Extended automorphism group of a Klein surface / reflections in dihedral groups
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (theory of NEC groups and Klein surfaces: Macbeath, Bujalance et al.)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful but classical classification of real structures on complex elliptic curves via lattice symmetries and dihedral groups. It is of mild historical interest as part of Grothendieck's 1983–84 conformal surgery program. The accompanying conjecture on the next page is actually incorrect except in the square-lattice case.
transcription_corrections: 'de la courbe elliptique complexe σ(Π,ℂ)' should likely read 'de la courbe elliptique complexe X définie par (Π, c)': G is the group of automorphisms σ of (Π, c) up to orientation.
'Pour que X admette une structure réelle, il faut et il suffit que G →det ±1 soit surjectif, et alors on a' is the intended reading of the passage around lines 9–11.

The lower passage reads approximately: 'Mais un élément σ de G de déterminant −1 est une transformation orth. de déterminant −1, et une telle est une réflexion, donc c'est une structure réelle sur la courbe elliptique : les courbes elliptiques qui admettent une structure réelle sont celles dont l'invariant modulaire est réel'. The fragment '$G^+$ est cyclique d'ordre' belongs to the following sentence: 'L'une [...] G^+, qui est cyclique d'ordre n = 2, 4, ou 6, et G est un groupe diédral ? Oui[?]. Étude des exemples aux groupes diédraux'.
The struck-out fragment near the end appears to be '(pour X générique)' with '±1' / '{±1}' related to G^+ in the generic case.
